speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you have a neck swelling; can you tell me how long it has been there and if it is painful to the touch?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck.

Based on your 50-year-old male patient presenting with a progressively increasing painless neck swelling on the nape of the neck for two months, combined with a history of colon cancer, diabetes, hypertension, and osteoarthritis, and current medications including insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen, the clinical picture is highly suggestive of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. The patient has denied fever, pain, or discharge, and the swelling has been present for two months. Given the history of colon cancer, metastasis to the neck is a concern, but the characteristics of the swelling (painless, progressive) are more consistent with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. To confirm the diagnosis, a biopsy of the neck swelling is necessary. REQUEST TEST: Biopsy of neck swelling.
